The most powerful refutation is that the felicific calculus falsely assumes all pleasures and pains are commensurable on a single quantitative scale, when in fact they differ irreducibly in kind and quality. This objection shows the calculus cannot capture what actually makes lives go well or badly, making it conceptually incoherent rather than merely impractical. The note’s suggested objection is weaker because it targets the universality of pleasure and pain, not the calculus’s core quantitative assumption.

CONFIDENCE: 92
